items.html:
Most utility poles in Mexico are made of concrete and have an octagonal shape. There will often be engravings on the side.

NOTE: Octagonal poles are also common in Colombia.

Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs. Front plates are required.

NOTE: For an overview of the most common regional designs, see step 2.

The most typical Mexican road lines are white solid outer lines with a single unbroken yellow middle line.

NOTE: Single broken yellow middle lines and double yellow middle lines are also common.
These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector can sometimes be seen, as well as a flat version.

Mexico has two general road shields; one for national highways with “MEXICO” written at the top and a slightly curvy design, and one for state roads which have straight borders, and typically has the state initials written at the top.
Mexican directional signs have a distinctly large, all-caps white font.
Mexican kilometre markers are white, with black font and outline.
Cacti, of many different species, are extremely common in Mexico.

Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs.

NOTE: All of South America, as well as Puerto Rico, use the word “PARE”. Panama, Costa Rica, and Guatemala also use “ALTO”.
Arrows on signs are noticeably very thick.
Yellow accents on kerbs and bridge barriers are quite common.
You will commonly see wide cylindrical, black or white water tanks on rooftops.

OXXO and Pemex are two of the most popular gas station brands in Mexico.

NOTE: While less common, OXXO can still be found in other countries.
Many place names in Mexico are of Nahuatl origin, featuring a lot of ‘x’ and ‘tl’ as well as ‘-ec’ and ‘-tlan’ suffixes.

Mexico uses circular electricity counters.

NOTE: Circular electricity counters are not unique to Mexico and can also be found in the US, Guatemala, Dominican Republic and the Philippines.
United States car brands are popular in Mexico. In particular, you will see a lot of pickup trucks.

Mexico is one of very few Latin American countries that has Generation 2 coverage.

NOTE: Brazil has some Generation 2, but it is considerably more rare, as most of it is overwritten.

The Generation 3 coverage in Mexico mainly feature two cars:

  • A white car with a stubby antenna. There is a diagonal coil wrapped around the antenna.
  • A white car with a more visible back and a long red brake light instead of an antenna.

It is possible to find a white car without a stubby antenna, but with a tiny sliver visible where the antenna should be.

The Generation 4 cars in Mexico commonly have a visible front and can feature various different colour patterns. The three most common ones are:

  • Blue
  • White with a blue stripe
  • Black
The first digit of Mexican area codes are regional and can be seen on this map.
Similarly, Mexican postal codes can be seen on this map. They will commonly appear at the bottom of street signs, and are ordered alphabetically based on state names.
Every state in Mexico has one or several unique licence plate designs. In this infographic you can find the most common and helpful ones.
Prickly pear cacti are distinct with their flat oval-shaped pads. They are noticeably more common centrally and are rarely seen in southern and coastal states.

Agave salmiana, also known as pulque agaves, have wide, smooth, curling leaves, and a crown-like appearance. They are common in the central Mexican valley and further north around the city of San Luis Potosi.
Vast fields of blue agave (Agave tequilana), used to produce tequila, are mostly found in Jalisco and Nayarit.

Yucca filifera, also known as tree yucca, as well as yucca decipiens are most commonly seen in San Luis Potosi and Zacatecas as well as some of the bordering northern states. They can be recognised by their oblong rosettes of sharp green leaves branching from a single trunk, similar to a tree.
The Mexican Giant Cardon is an extremely common cacti in the Baja California peninsula. It can be identified through its large sprawling arms stemming from a singular trunk and ribbed exterior.
The Saguaro Cacti can be spotted in the western half of Sonora, featuring short curving arms that stem from a main trunk.
Organ Pipe Cacti have long thin stems that often come out from a stem that is around ground level. They are most commonly found in Sonora and occasionally in Baja California Sur.
The Blue Myrtle Cacti have short arms that uniformly curve and point upwards. It is abundantly found in San Luis Potosi, but also common in Queretaro and Hidalgo.
Sugar cane can be found all over the country, but by far most common in Veracruz.
Coconut palms can be found all across the coast, but are often found in large groups in Guerrero and Colima.

Sabal palms are most commonly observed in the east coast of Mexico, the Yucatan peninsula, as well as the state of Nayarit. They feature a spiky, sun-shaped crown, giving the tree a lollipop-like appearance.
The Attalea rostrata is a huge palm recognizable from its upright leaves, almost resembling an umbrella. It is mostly exclusive to Veracruz and Tabasco, and can be rarely found in Chiapas.
Oil palm plantations are most common in Chiapas, and occasionally on the outskirts of the state in Veracruz, Tabasco, and Campeche.
Boojum trees can be recognized by their alien, tentacle-like appearance. They are almost exclusively found in the southern half of Baja California.
Brittlebush are small shrubs with bright silver-grey leaves that are most commonly found in Sonora, especially around Hermosillo.
These thin, white-barked trees can be found in the Yucatan peninsula, but are most prevalent in Quintana Roo.
These gold tufts of grass in a line right next to the road are most commonly found in Coahuila.
These clumps of grass in almost a teardrop shape are common in the region around Tlaxcala.
Red agricultural fields are commonly seen in Zacatecas and occasionally southern Durango.
The Monterrey metropolitan area features tall stunning mountain ranges that surround the city.

The western parts of Chihuahua and Durango can feature a rocky mountainous landscape covered with pine forests. In general, these pines are shorter and more stunted in appearance than pine forests of the central or south.
Extremely dark fields are common in Guanajuato.
These reddish brown-tinged hills, often accompanied by large boulders, are a common sight for the northern half of Baja California.

Almost blindingly white soil in the Yucatan peninsula is most common in Quintana Roo.

NOTE: This is only consistent in Generation 3.
These red agricultural fields surrounded by dense forests of tropical trees are most common in northern Campeche.
Red brick buildings are mostly concentrated in the states west of Mexico City, specifically Jalisco, Michoacan, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes.
White concrete block buildings are highly concentrated in the states surrounding Mexico city, and are generally more common to the east. They can however still be found all over the country.
Mud brick buildings are most abundant in Durango, especially full houses constructed with mud brick. However, they can essentially be found in almost all of the dry desert states.

Architecture in northern Mexico often features design elements from American style bungalows. Many houses are coloured with light or pastel colours, gated and commonly have front yards. Orange tiles inspired by Spanish colonial architecture are also typical.
Thatched roofs are most common in the Yucatan peninsula and eastern San Luis Potosi. They can also be found elsewhere, mainly in the southeast.
These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.
A thick cross can be seen on the back of signs in Chihuahua.
Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.
Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.
White insulators that are shaped like acorns can be found along the coastal states of Mexico, but are by far most common in Michoacan, Colima, and Veracruz.
Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.
Wooden poles with a lowered crossbar are mostly found in Sinaloa and Sonora.
These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.
The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.
Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.
Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.
White middle roadlines are most commonly found in Tabasco.

These fences made out of trees with red-coloured bark are commonly found in Veracruz.

NOTE: These tree fences can still be found in other coastal states and are best utilised when combined with other clues.

Black tar on both sides of the yellow centre line can be seen in Sinaloa, Durango, and Guerrero.

NOTE: This is most reliable when the tar is not faded.

Grainy pavement with a blue-ish grey tinge is a common sight for the states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon.

NOTE: In Tamaulipas, larger roads very commonly feature dashed outer lines.

This style of cobblestone pavement, unorganised with irregular tiles, can be found in most of the central states, but is by far most commonly found in the states of Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, and Queretaro.
This pavement consisting of hexagonal tiles is found in Puebla and Tlaxcala.
This exact pavement design with three lines of cobblestone patterning is mainly found in Oaxaca.
Taxis in and around Mexico City have a white lower half with a pink upper half.
The area around Mexicali features flat farmland with a ridge to the west. Washingtonia palms are very common and these poles made out of brown wood can be found.
The area around Poza Rica in Veracruz features a lot of citrus tree plantations. It is common to see large amounts of these trees grown right on top of the hills.
The area around Ciudad Obregon is distinct due to the pinkish-tan soil and canals found around the city’s agricultural areas.

The twin volcanoes of Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl are found on the border between the State of Mexico and Puebla. Keep in mind that they are usually much less visible than depicted in the image, which is just for reference.
Cerro del Bernal is a distinct extinct volcano that is found in southern Tamaulipas. It can be found heading directly northwest of Tampico or west of Morón.
This extremely long and flat ridge is found in the Sierra del Abra Tanchipa Biosphere Reserve in eastern San Luis Potosi.

This tall, flat ridge, with very prominent ridgelines, belongs to the Maderas del Carmen Biosphere Reserve in Northern Coahuila near the US border.

NOTE: The only road the mountain range can be observed from is the Federal Highway 53 that leads to Boquillas del Carmen.
The outskirts of Ciudad Juárez features a lot of dirt roads with a distinct shade of orange soil and low shrubs.

The area around San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca and south of it in Oaxaca often feature rolling hills with really distinct orange and beige-tinged soil, passing from one colour to the other with each hill. The beige-tinged soil can be seen more prominent in some locations.

The town of Guaymas has a lot of jagged cliffs and mountains that make the area very distinct. The soil is also distinctly pinkish and organ-pipe cacti can be seen scattered on the hills and next to the road.
The town of Las Coloradas is famously known for the pink lakes around the area.

The 54 is a divided highway that runs through northeastern Zacatecas which features yucca trees spammed on both sides of the road. Additionally, the streetview car is often exposed and appears almost white due to the sunlight.

The 40D that crosses the Sinaloa-Durango state line is recognizable by the stunning lush cliffs and mountains along the road. The highway commonly passes through tunnels and the road itself features double yellow middle roadlines.
This road divider with a yellow top and bottom edge is found all along the 95D from Mexico City to Acapulco.
The Eurus Wind Farm is located in southeast Oaxaca and is the largest wind farm in Mexico. Rows of wind turbines can be found along the 190 around Juchitán de Zaragoza.

Most lamp posts and lamp arms in Aguascalientes city are yellow.

NOTE: They are not exclusive and are only very common.
This lamp with a black rectangular head is found in Cuernavaca.
This lamp with black front and back edges and a white middle section is found in Santiago de Queretaro.
This lamp with five circular bulbs that looks like a dice is found in Cancun.
This lamp with a rectangular head and a ring-shaped light bulb is found in Matamoros.
This lamp with a zig-zag bent pole arm is found in Hermosillo.

The bottom half of poles in Cuernavaca are often painted green.

NOTE: In Generation 4, the paint usually looks faded, some to the point where it is barely visible.
Poles in Chihuahua city occasionally have a strip of white pole paint with the street name written in black or blue text.
This Street View car with a yellow hood can be found by the La Malinche volcano in Tlaxcala.
This white truck with visible rearview mirrors can be seen in the Cofre de Perote national park.
This red Street View car with a black roof can be found in the town of La Seca in Sinaloa.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • AI Gen - Mexico (map link) - 80k+ AI generated locations in Mexico. May not be pinpointable. This map is also used for Plonk Its official Mexico state streak leaderboard.
  • An Arbitrary Mexico (map link) - 120k+ non-pinpointable balanced AI generated locations in Mexico.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Mexico:

  • Plonk It Mexico (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Mexico guide from step 2 to 3.
  • Mexico License Plates Practise (map link) - Map to practise Mexican licence plates.

lm.name: Mexico
lm.note:
Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs. Front plates are required.

NOTE: For an overview of the most common regional designs, see this image.

lm.name: Agriculture - Blue Agave
lm.note:
Commonly known as the blue agave, A. tequilana is immediately recognisable by its blue, sharply protruding leaves. This is the agave from which tequila is extracted, and it mainly inhabits Jalisco, where it is almost always observed in magnificent fields which can even coalesce into vast shades of blue from a distance.

Similar, but different: A. anguistifolia.

While it is difficult to distinguish them, A. tequilana is noticeably bluer. One other difference is that A. angustifolia is more commonly spotted in isolated groupings than A. tequilana, but expansive fields still exist.

lm.name: Agriculture - Campeche Fields
lm.note: These red agricultural fields surrounded by dense forests of tropical trees are most common in northern Campeche.

lm.name: Agriculture - Citrus Tree Plantation
lm.note: The area around Poza Rica in Veracruz features a lot of citrus tree plantations. It is common to see large amounts of these trees grown right on top of the hills.

lm.name: Agriculture - Oil Palm
lm.note: Oil palm plantations are most common in Chiapas, and occasionally on the outskirts of the state in Veracruz, Tabasco, and Campeche.

lm.name: Agriculture - Prickly Pear Farm
lm.note: In the northeast most area of State of Mexico, around the town Nopaltepec, they often farm Opuntia in vast plains. Farms of prickly pear are otherwise most commonly found in north east Morelos, where they foreground striking, sculpturally eroded dry hills. These farms can be found randomly elsewhere in the country, but much less commonly; if there is a third most common location for them it would be Guanajuato.

lm.name: Agriculture - Pulque Agave Field
lm.note: One will often notice scattered farms of A. salmiana, gatherings which stretch limitlessly in neat rows; these will almost always be found around the city of Pachuca in Hidalgo, and rarely more south-east.

lm.name: Agriculture - Red Agricultural Fields
lm.note: Red agricultural fields are commonly seen in Zacatecas and occasionally southern Durango.

lm.name: Agriculture - Sugarcane
lm.note: Sugarcane can be found all over the country, but by far most common in Veracruz.

lm.name: Agriculture - Very Dark Fields
lm.note: Extremely dark fields are common in Guanajuato.

lm.name: Architecture - Mud Brick
lm.note: Mud brick buildings are most abundant in Durango, especially full houses constructed with mud brick. However, they can essentially be found in almost all of the dry desert states.

lm.name: Architecture - Northern Mexico Architecture
lm.note: Architecture in northern Mexico often features design elements from American style bungalows. Many houses are coloured with light or pastel colours, gated and commonly have front yards. Orange tiles inspired by Spanish colonial architecture are also typical.

lm.name: Architecture - Red Brick
lm.note: Red brick buildings are mostly concentrated in the states west of Mexico City, specifically Jalisco, Michoacan, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes.

lm.name: Architecture - Thatched Roof
lm.note: Thatched roofs are most common in the Yucatan peninsula and eastern San Luis Potosi. They can also be found elsewhere, mainly in the southeast.

lm.name: Architecture - White Concrete Blocks
lm.note: White concrete block buildings are highly concentrated in the states surrounding Mexico city, and are generally more common to the east. They can however still be found all over the country.

lm.name: Car Meta - Cofre de Perote Truck
lm.note: This white truck with visible rearview mirrors can be seen in the Cofre de Perote national park.

lm.name: Car Meta - La Malinche Car
lm.note: This Street View car with a yellow hood can be found by the La Malinche volcano in Tlaxcala.

lm.name: Car Meta - La Seca Car
lm.note: This red Street View car with a black roof can be found in the town of La Seca in Sinaloa.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Asymmetric & Double-Stacked Insulator
lm.note: Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Black Tar
lm.note:
Black tar on both sides of the yellow centre line can be seen in Sinaloa, Durango, and Guerrero.

NOTE: This is most reliable when the tar is not faded.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Blue Grain Pavement
lm.note:
Grainy pavement with a blue-ish grey tinge is a common sight for the states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon.

NOTE: In Tamaulipas, larger roads very commonly feature dashed outer lines.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cancun Lamp
lm.note: This lamp with five circular bulbs that looks like a dice is found in Cancun.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CDMX Taxi
lm.note: Taxis in and around Mexico City have a white lower half with a pink upper half.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Chihuahua Cross
lm.note: A thick cross can be seen on the back of signs in Chihuahua.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Chihuahua Pole Paint
lm.note: Poles in Chihuahua city occasionally have a strip of white pole paint with the street name written in black or blue text.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cobblestone
lm.note: This style of cobblestone pavement, unorganised with irregular tiles, can be found in most of the central states, but is by far most commonly found in the states of Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, and Queretaro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cuernavaca Lamp
lm.note: This lamp with a black rectangular head is found in Cuernavaca.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Durango Pole
lm.note: Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Eurus Wind Farm
lm.note: The Eurus Wind Farm is located in southeast Oaxaca and is the largest wind farm in Mexico. Rows of wind turbines can be found along the 190 around Juchitán de Zaragoza.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Green Bottom Pole
lm.note:
The bottom half of poles in Cuernavaca are often painted green.

NOTE: In Generation 4, the paint usually looks faded, some to the point where it is barely visible.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Hanging Insulator (Concrete)
lm.note: These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Hanging Insulator (Wooden)
lm.note: The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Hexagonal Tiles
lm.note: This pavement consisting of hexagonal tiles is found in Puebla and Tlaxcala.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Jalisco Bollard
lm.note: Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Light Rock Wall
lm.note: These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Matamoros Lamp
lm.note: This lamp with a rectangular head and a ring-shaped light bulb is found in Matamoros.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Mesh Pole
lm.note: Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Nayarit Bollard
lm.note: Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Oaxaca Pavement
lm.note: This exact pavement design with three lines of cobblestone patterning is exclusive to Oaxaca.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Santiago de Queretaro Lamp
lm.note: This lamp with black front and back edges and a white middle section is found in Santiago de Queretaro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tree Fences
lm.note:
These fences made out of trees with red-coloured bark are commonly found in Veracruz.

NOTE: These tree fences can still be found in other coastal states and are best utilised when combined with other clues.

lm.name: Infrastructure - White Acorn Insulator
lm.note: White insulators that are shaped like acorns can be found along the coastal states of Mexico, but are by far most common in Michoacan, Colima, and Veracruz.

lm.name: Infrastructure - White Roadlines
lm.note: White middle roadlines are most commonly found in Tabasco.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Wooden & Low Crossbar
lm.note: Wooden poles with a lowered crossbar are mostly found in Sinaloa and Sonora.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Edge Road Divider
lm.note: This road divider with a yellow top and bottom edge is found all along the 95D from Mexico City to Acapulco.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Lamp Post
lm.note:
Most lamp posts and lamp arms in Aguascalientes city are yellow.

NOTE: They are not exclusive and are only very common.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Zig-Zag Lamp
lm.note: This lamp with a zig-zag bent pole arm is found in Hermosillo.

lm.name: Landscape - Cerro del Bernal
lm.note: Cerro del Bernal is a distinct extinct volcano that is found in southern Tamaulipas. It can be found heading directly northwest of Tampico or west of Morón.

lm.name: Landscape - Ciudad Juarez
lm.note: The outskirts of Ciudad Juárez features a lot of dirt roads with a distinct shade of orange soil and low shrubs.

lm.name: Landscape - Ciudad Obregon
lm.note: The area around Ciudad Obregon is distinct due to the pinkish-tan soil and canals found around the city’s agricultural areas.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Cactus
lm.note: If you see a cactus in a coastal area, you're probably in Oaxaca.

lm.name: Landscape - Guaymas Cliffs
lm.note: The town of Guaymas has a lot of jagged cliffs and mountains that make the area very distinct. The soil is also distinctly pinkish and organ-pipe cacti can be seen scattered on the hills and next to the road.

lm.name: Landscape - Maderas del Carmen
lm.note:
This tall, flat ridge, with very prominent ridgelines, belongs to the Maderas del Carmen Biosphere Reserve in Northern Coahuila near the US border.

NOTE: The only road the mountain range can be observed from is the Federal Highway 53 that leads to Boquillas del Carmen.

lm.name: Landscape - MEX-40D
lm.note: The 40D that crosses the Sinaloa-Durango state line is recognizable by the stunning lush cliffs and mountains along the road. The highway commonly passes through tunnels and the road itself features double yellow middle roadlines.

lm.name: Landscape - MEX-54
lm.note: The 54 is a divided highway that runs through northeastern Zacatecas which features yucca trees spammed on both sides of the road. Additionally, the streetview car is often exposed and appears almost white due to the sunlight.

lm.name: Landscape - Mexicali Landscape
lm.note: The area around Mexicali features flat farmland with a ridge to the west. Washingtonia palms are very common and these poles made out of brown wood can be found.

lm.name: Landscape - Monterrey Mountains
lm.note: The Monterrey metropolitan area features tall stunning mountain ranges that surround the city.

lm.name: Landscape - Morelos Prickly Pear Farms
lm.note: Farms of prickly pear are commonly found in north east Morelos, where they foreground **striking, sculpturally eroded dry hills. **

lm.name: Landscape - Northern Baja Landscape
lm.note: These reddish brown-tinged hills, often accompanied by large boulders, are a common sight for the northern half of Baja California.

lm.name: Landscape - Pink Lakes
lm.note: The town of Los Coloradas is famously known for the pink lakes around the area.

lm.name: Landscape - San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca
lm.note: The area around San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca and south of it in Oaxaca often feature rolling hills with really distinct orange and beige-tinged soil, passing from one colour to the other with each hill. The beige-tinged soil can be seen more prominent in some locations.

lm.name: Landscape - Sierra del Abra Tanchipa
lm.note: This extremely long and flat ridge is found in the Sierra del Abra Tanchipa Biosphere Reserve in eastern San Luis Potosi.

lm.name: Landscape - Twin Volcanoes
lm.note: The twin volcanoes of Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl are found on the border between the State of Mexico and Puebla. Keep in mind that they are usually much less visible than depicted in the image, which is just for reference.

lm.name: Landscape - Western Chi/Dur Landscape
lm.note: The western parts of Chihuahua and Durango can feature a rocky mountainous landscape covered with pine forests. In general, these pines are shorter and more stunted in appearance than pine forests of the central or south.

lm.name: Landscape - White Soil
lm.note:
Almost blindingly white soil in the Yucatan peninsula is most common in Quintana Roo.

NOTE: This is only consistent in Generation 3.

lm.name: Vegetation - Agave angustifolia
lm.note:
blue, but less blue than tequilana, smaller grouping

found in Central Oaxaca

lm.name: Vegetation - Agave Asperrina
lm.note: The rough century plant looks similar to the pulque agave but its leaves are blueish and it is much smaller. It is distributed nearly identically to A. lechuguilla (Durango and Coahuila, especially around Saltillo and West of Torreon, rarely SLP and Hidalgo), and is often difficult to spot from the road, only barely visible in the distance in batches.

lm.name: Vegetation - Agave Cupreata
lm.note: Agave cupreata is a very rarely observed agave that is localised to central Guerrero. Its name is apt - it has a much more pronounced, cup-like appearance than other agaves, with the leaves lurching inwards. It is often found growing on walls in groups as depicted.

lm.name: Vegetation - Agave Karwinskii
lm.note: A. karwinskii is exclusively seen in the central desert region of Oaxaca, mostly near the town Miahuatlán de Porfirio Díaz, even though technically its native distribution extends elsewhere in the state and barely into Puebla. Its spiky thin leaves, protruding from the centre in a cylindrical formation, make it quite distinct from other common agaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - Agave Lechuguilla
lm.note: Agave lechuguilla is a very frequent sighting in the hills of Durango and Coahuila, particularly around the cities of Saltillo and west of Torreon. More rarely it can be found in San Luis Potosi and Hidalgo. It is distinguished by its slick, lime-green leaves that almost look as if they are combed to one side.

lm.name: Vegetation - Blue Myrtle Cactus
lm.note: Myrtillocactus Geometrizans is a species of cactus in the genus Myrtillocactus, native to central and northern Mexico. It is especially abundant in San Luis Potosi, but also common in Queretaro and Hidalgo, and much more rarely Guanajuato.

lm.name: Vegetation - Boojum Tree
lm.note: Boojum trees can be recognized by their alien, tentacle-like appearance. They are almost exclusively found in the southern half of Baja California.

lm.name: Vegetation - Brittlebush
lm.note: Brittlebush are small shrubs with bright silver-grey leaves that are most commonly found in Sonora, especially around Hermosillo.

lm.name: Vegetation - Candelabro
lm.note: Pachycereus weberi is widespread in the Mexican states of Puebla, Guerrero, Morelos, Hidalgo and Oaxaca at altitudes of 600 to 1,500 m.

lm.name: Vegetation - Cephalocereus Mezcalaensis
lm.note: This tall, columnar cactus, with no branches, is native to northern Oaxaca and southern Puebla, and another of the many species present there. Much less commonly but still possibly it can be seen in central Guerrero.

lm.name: Vegetation - Chiotilla
lm.note: The species originates from Mexico (Guerrero, Michoacán, Oaxaca, southern Puebla). It will almost always place you somewhere in Oaxaca, usually central in the state.

lm.name: Vegetation - Coconut Palm
lm.note: Coconut palms can be found all across the coast, but are often found in large groups in Guerrero and Colima.

lm.name: Vegetation - Florida Thach palm
lm.note:
This palm is recognizable through its round fan leaves.

Within Mexico, it's usually found in Yucatan.

lm.name: Vegetation - Fruit Cholla
lm.note: The golden glow of the fruit cholla is also unmistakable, and present mostly in the Western Half of Sonora.

lm.name: Vegetation - Giant Cardon
lm.note: Pachycereus pringlei is a species of large cactus native to northwestern Mexico, in the states of Baja California, Baja California Sur. It can rarely be found on the Sonoran coast, around the area south of Puerto Libertad on the 3.

lm.name: Vegetation - Golden Line
lm.note: These gold tufts of grass in a line right next to the road are most commonly found in Coahuila.

lm.name: Vegetation - Indian Comb
lm.note: The Indian Comb (Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum), is a common cactus that always implies Sinaloa, or south Sonora near Sinaloa, although technically its habitat extends elsewhere. Its densely packed branches emerge from a single stem, but most recognisable is its inflorescence - the brightly coloured flowers which usually adorn the tip of its arms.

lm.name: Vegetation - Organ Pipe Cactus
lm.note: This species is found mostly in Mexico, mainly in Sonora and southern Baja California and Northern Sinaloa. If the cactus is significantly larger than 3m, it's probably in Southern Baja.

lm.name: Vegetation - Organ Pipe Spam
lm.note: A huge abundance of Organ Pipe Cacti it is usually indicative of the reserve El Cajón del Diablo, south of Hermosillo.

lm.name: Vegetation - Pitaya de Querétaro
lm.note:
In Pitaya the branches less organically sprout from the ground in the weed-like manner of the Organ Pipe, and instead curl smoothly outwards from a central stem.

It is mostly found in Jalisco, south of Guadalajara. Less commonly, it's seen in Guanajuato. It can be seen in Queretaro too, but surprisingly rarely.

lm.name: Vegetation - Prickly Pear alone
lm.note: Prickly pear cacti with a total absence of other cacti, yucca, agaves or in general succulent plants except for the prickly pear is generally a good signal for the centre-west (Jalisco, Guanajuato, Michoacan).

lm.name: Vegetation - Prickly Pear Cactus
lm.note:
Prickly pear cacti are distinct with their flat oval-shaped pads. They are noticeably more common centrally and are rarely seen in southern and coastal states.

They are also good for some 50/50:

  • Durango > Chihuahua
  • Durango > Sonora (less reliable)
  • Nuevo Leon > Tamaulipas
  • Other States > Mexico State

lm.name: Vegetation - Pulque Agave
lm.note:
Agave salmiana, colloquially the pulque agave, is native to central Mexico. Agaves in general are distinguishable by their crown-like appearance, with stiff leaves which fan outwards symmetrically. The pulque agave is no different, but has green leaves, relatively smooth edges, and flat leaves that curl slightly away from the central axis.

Note its distribution, in an arc around Mexico City and a second pocket of endemism which straddles San Luis Potosi city and Aguascalientes.

lm.name: Vegetation - Quintana Roo Tree
lm.note: These thin, white-barked trees can be found in the Yucatan peninsula, but are most prevalent in Quintana Roo.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Mexicana
lm.note:
This palm seems to be prominent in coastal Texas, the east and the south coast of Mexico, Yucatán peninsula, and Guatemala. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips. Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Rosei
lm.note:
Sabal Rosei is native to the Pacific coast of Mexico, from Sinaloa to Jalisco but mostly concentrated in the state of Nayarit. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips. Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Yapa
lm.note:
This palm grows pretty much exclusively in the Yucatán peninsula. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips.

Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed. Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

lm.name: Vegetation - Saguaro
lm.note: The Saguaro is endemic to the Sonoran Desert and is found primarily in western Sonora in Mexico, and in western Arizona in the US. Elevation is a limiting factor to its environment, as the saguaro is sensitive to extended frost or cold temperatures.

lm.name: Vegetation - Stenocereus fricii
lm.note: A rare and tall cactus, the thin and twirling branches of S. fricii are unique to Michoacan, especially on the 37D, where it is abundantly spammed.

lm.name: Vegetation - Tlaxcala Bois
lm.note: These clumps of grass in almost a teardrop shape are common in the region around Tlaxcala.

lm.name: Vegetation - Tree Cholla
lm.note:
The tree cholla is a cactus, and its skeletal, discoloured arms spurting in every direction make it recognisable.

Mostly found in San Luis Potosi, Queretaro and Hidalgo, often in Coahuila and Durango and rarely in Zacatecas.

lm.name: Vegetation - Tree Cholla Group
lm.note: If it is present in groups, Tree Cholla is usually a good indication of San Luis Potosi.

lm.name: Vegetation - Tree Yucca
lm.note: It is native to central mexico, most commonly found in Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí although it can be seen anywhere from Nuevo León down to Puebla, in dry regions.

lm.name: Vegetation - Umbrella Palm
lm.note: The Attalea rostrata is a huge palm recognizable from its upright leaves, almost resembling an umbrella. It is mostly exclusive to Veracruz and Tabasco, and can be rarely found in Chiapas.

lm.name: Vegetation - Unknown Cactus
lm.note: Oaxaca is very diverse in Cacti, so if you see a strange cactus, or one that isn't explained in this map, you can consider going Oaxaca.

lm.name: Agave salmiana
lm.note: Agave salmiana, also known as pulque agaves, have wide, smooth, curling leaves, and a crown-like appearance. They are common in the central Mexican valley and further north around the city of San Luis Potosi.

lm.name: Agave tequilana
lm.note: Vast fields of blue agave (Agave tequilana), used to produce tequila, are mostly found in Jalisco and Nayarit.

lm.name: Asymmetric mushroom-like insulator pole
lm.note: Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.

lm.name: Black tar
lm.note:
Black tar on both sides of the yellow centre line can be seen in Sinaloa, Durango, and Guerrero.

NOTE: This is most reliable when the tar is not faded.

lm.name: Blindingly white soil
lm.note:
Almost blindingly white soil in the Yucatan peninsula is most common in Quintana Roo.

NOTE: This is only consistent in Generation 3.

lm.name: Blue Myrtle Cacti
lm.note: The Blue Myrtle Cacti have short arms that uniformly curve and point upwards. It is abundantly found in San Luis Potosi, but also common in Queretaro and Hidalgo.

lm.name: Boojum trees
lm.note: Boojum trees can be recognized by their alien, tentacle-like appearance. They are almost exclusively found in the southern half of Baja California.

lm.name: Brittlebush
lm.note: Brittlebush are small shrubs with bright silver-grey leaves that are most commonly found in Sonora, especially around Hermosillo.

lm.name: Chihuahua cross
lm.note: A thick cross can be seen on the back of signs in Chihuahua.

lm.name: Coahuila gold tufts
lm.note: These gold tufts of grass in a line right next to the road are most commonly found in Coahuila.

lm.name: Cobblestone pavement
lm.note: This style of cobblestone pavement, unorganised with irregular tiles, can be found in most of the central states, but is by far most commonly found in the states of Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, and Queretaro.

lm.name: Concrete hanging insulator pole
lm.note: These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.

lm.name: Giant Cardon
lm.note: The Mexican Giant Cardon is an extremely common cacti in the Baja California peninsula. It can be identified through its large sprawling arms stemming from a singular trunk and ribbed exterior.

lm.name: Grainy pavement
lm.note:
Grainy pavement with a blue-ish grey tinge is a common sight for the states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon.

NOTE: In Tamaulipas, larger roads very commonly feature dashed outer lines.

lm.name: Guanajuato extremely dark fields
lm.note: Extremely dark fields are common in Guanajuato.

lm.name: Hexagonal tiles pavement
lm.note: This pavement consisting of hexagonal tiles is found in Puebla and Tlaxcala.

lm.name: Jalisco bollards
lm.note: Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.

lm.name: Light coloured rock walls
lm.note:
These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.

Comment from Vincent: When not in the sun, the rock walls appear darker, but it's likely the same type of rock.

lm.name: Mesh body pole
lm.note: Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.

lm.name: Nayarit bollard
lm.note: Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.

lm.name: Oaxaca pavement
lm.note: This exact pavement design with three lines of cobblestone patterning is exclusive to Oaxaca.

lm.name: Oil palm plantations
lm.note: Oil palm plantations are most common in Chiapas, and occasionally on the outskirts of the state in Veracruz, Tabasco, and Campeche.

lm.name: Red agricultural fields
lm.note: Red agricultural fields are commonly seen in Zacatecas and occasionally southern Durango.

lm.name: Saguaro Cacti
lm.note: The Saguaro Cacti can be spotted in the western half of Sonora, featuring short curving arms that stem from a main trunk.

lm.name: Western, shorter pine forest
lm.note: The western parts of Chihuahua and Durango can feature a rocky mountainous landscape covered with pine forests. In general, these pines are shorter and more stunted in appearance than pine forests of the central or south.

lm.name: White middle roadlines
lm.note: White middle roadlines are most commonly found in Tabasco.

lm.name: Wooden hanging insulator pole
lm.note: The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.

lm.name: Yucca filifera
lm.note: Yucca filifera, also known as tree yucca, as well as yucca decipiens are most commonly seen in San Luis Potosi and Zacatecas as well as some of the bordering northern states. They can be recognised by their oblong rosettes of sharp green leaves branching from a single trunk, similar to a tree.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Stop Signs
lm.name: Alto
lm.note: Mexico, Panama, Costa Rica and Guatemala are the only countries using the word "Alto" on their stop signs.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: ALTO
lm.note:
• Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs.

--- NOTE:

  • All of South America uses the word “PARE”.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Black & White Water Tanks
lm.note: • You will commonly see wide cylindrical, black or white water tanks on rooftops.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Bollards
lm.note: • These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector can sometimes be seen, as well as a flat version.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Cacti
lm.note: • Cacti, of many different species, are extremely common in Mexico.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Electricity Counters
lm.note:
• Mexico uses circular electricity counters.

--- NOTE:

  • Circular electricity counters are not unique to Mexico and can also be found in the US, Guatemala, Dominican Republic and the Philippines.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Gen 3 Cars
lm.note:
The Generation 3 coverage in Mexico mainly feature two cars:

  • A white car with a stubby antenna.
  • A white car with a more visible back and a long red brake light

--- NOTE:

  • It is possible to find a white car without a stubby antenna, but with a tiny sliver visible where the antenna should be.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: License Plates
lm.note:
• Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs.
  • Front plates are required.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Octagonal Pole
lm.note:
• Most utility poles in Mexico are made of concrete and have an octagonal shape.
  • There will often be engravings on the side.

--- NOTE:

  • Octagonal poles are also common in Colombia.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Thick Arrows
lm.note: • Arrows on signs are noticeably very thick.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note: These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector is sometimes seen, as well as a flat version.

lm.name: Jalisco Bollard
lm.note: Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.

lm.name: Nayarit Bollard
lm.note: Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.

lm.name: Campeche Fields
lm.note: These red agricultural fields surrounded by dense forests of tropical trees are most common in northern Campeche.

lm.name: Cerro Del Bernal
lm.note: Cerro del Bernal is a distinct extinct volcano that is found in southern Tamaulipas. It can be found heading directly northwest of Tampico or west of Morón.

lm.name: Ciudad Juárez Outskirts
lm.note: The outskirts of Ciudad Juárez features a lot of dirt roads with a distinct shade of orange soil and low shrubs.

lm.name: Guanajuato Dark Fields
lm.note: Extremely dark fields are common in Guanajuato.

lm.name: Guaymas Mountains
lm.note: The town of Guaymas has a lot of jagged cliffs and mountains that make the area very distinct. The soil is also distinctly pinkish and organ-pipe cacti can be seen scattered on the hills and next to the road.

lm.name: Los Coloradas Pink Lakes
lm.note: The town of Los Coloradas is famously known for the pink lakes around the area.

lm.name: Maderas del Carmen Biosphere Reserve Ridge
lm.note: This tall, flat ridge, with very prominent ridgelines, belongs to the Maderas del Carmen Biosphere Reserve in Northern Coahuila near the US border. NOTE: The only road the mountain range can be observed from is the Federal Highway 53 that leads to Boquillas del Carmen.

lm.name: Mexicali Farmland
lm.note: The area around Mexicali features flat farmland with a ridge to the west. Washingtonia palms are very common and these poles made out of brown wood can be found.

lm.name: Monterrey Mountains
lm.note: The Monterrey metropolitan area features tall stunning mountain ranges that surround the city.

lm.name: North Baja California Hills
lm.note: These reddish brown-tinged hills, often accompanied by large boulders, are a common sight for the northern half of Baja California.

lm.name: Rocky Mountains
lm.note: The western parts of Chihuahua and Durango can feature a rocky mountainous landscape covered with pine forests. In general, these pines are shorter and more stunted in appearance than pine forests of the central or south.

lm.name: San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca Hills
lm.note: The area around San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca and south of it in Oaxaca often feature rolling hills with really distinct orange and beige-tinged soil, passing from one colour to the other with each hill. The beige-tinged soil can be seen more prominent in some locations.

lm.name: Sierra del Abra Tanchipa Biosphere Reserve
lm.note: This extremely long and flat ridge is found in the Sierra del Abra Tanchipa Biosphere Reserve in eastern San Luis Potosi.

lm.name: Twin Volcanoes
lm.note: The twin volcanoes of Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl are found on the border between the State of Mexico and Puebla. Keep in mind that they are usually much less visible than depicted in the image, which is just for reference.

lm.name: Zacatecas Red Fields
lm.note: Red agricultural fields are commonly seen in Zacatecas and occasionally southern Durango.

lm.name: East - White Concrete Blocks
lm.note:
• White concrete block buildings are highly concentrated in the states surrounding Mexico city, and are generally more common to the east.
  • They can however still be found all over the country.

lm.name: North - American Style Bungalows
lm.note:
• Architecture in northern Mexico often features design elements from American style bungalows.
  • Many houses are coloured with light or pastel colours, gated and commonly have front yards.
  • Orange tiles inspired by Spanish colonial architecture are also typical.

lm.name: West - Red Bricks
lm.note: • Red brick buildings are mostly concentrated in the states west of Mexico City, specifically Jalisco, Michoacan, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes.

lm.name: Durango - Mud Bricks
lm.note:
• Mud brick buildings are most abundant in Durango, especially full houses constructed with mud brick.
  • However, they can essentially be found in almost all of the dry desert states.

lm.name: Yucatan - Light Colored Rocks
lm.note: • These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.

lm.name: Yucatan - Thatched Roofs
lm.note:
• Thatched roofs are most common in the Yucatan peninsula and eastern San Luis Potosi.
  • They can also be found elsewhere, mainly in the southeast.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Intermediate
lm.name: Rounded electric counter
lm.note:
Mexico uses those circular electricity counters.

You can find those in other countries:

  • Philippines(vegetation,climate will be different)
  • USA(looks different,English instead of Spanish etc)
  • Guatamela(has car meta)
  • Dominican Republic(has car meta)

lm.name: Vegetation - Blue Myrtle Cactus
lm.note: Myrtillocactus Geometrizans is a species of cactus in the genus Myrtillocactus, native to central and northern Mexico. It is especially abundant in San Luis Potosi, but also common in Queretaro and Hidalgo, and much more rarely Guanajuato.

lm.name: Vegetation - Candelabro
lm.note: Pachycereus weberi is widespread in the Mexican states of Puebla, Guerrero, Morelos, Hidalgo and Oaxaca at altitudes of 600 to 1,500 m.

lm.name: Vegetation - Chiotilla
lm.note: The species originates from Mexico (Guerrero, Michoacán, Oaxaca, southern Puebla). It will almost always place you somewhere in Oaxaca, usually central in the state.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Mexicana
lm.note:
This palm seems to be prominent in coastal Texas, the east and the south coast of Mexico, Yucatán peninsula, and Guatemala. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips. Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Rosei
lm.note:
Sabal Rosei is native to the Pacific coast of Mexico, from Sinaloa to Jalisco but mostly concentrated in the state of Nayarit. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips. Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sabal Yapa
lm.note:
This palm grows pretty much exclusively in the Yucatán peninsula. The key difference between this one and the other Sabal palms is the shape and arrangement of the leaves.

Sabal Yapa has droopy, hanging leaves that almost look shredded at the tips.

Sabal Mexicana has large, stiff, pointy leaves and densely packed. Sabal Rosei tends to have visible gaps between the leaves, and they are a brighter green color.

lm.name: Aguascalientes - Aguascalientes
lm.note: This plate features a thin orange stripe along the top and another along the bottom, making it relatively straightforward to identify among Mexican state plates. The center of the plate is white, with a faint round symbol visible in the background. Note that this is an older plate design, so you will mostly encounter it in older Street View coverage. The vast majority of plates from this state are generation 3.

lm.name: Baja California blue - Baja California blue-green
lm.note: This plate is characterized by a blue stripe at the top and a light-blue center. The bottom typically displays a green stripe. In short, the overall color scheme is blue and green. Occasionally, a distinct dot is visible on the left side of the plate.

lm.name: Baja California Orange - Baja California Orange Green
lm.note: This plate features an orange stripe at the top and a light-blue center. The bottom typically displays a green stripe. Overall, the color scheme combines orange, blue, and green. As with the other Baja California variant, a distinct dot is occasionally visible on the left side of the plate.

lm.name: Baja california red - Baja california red
lm.note: This plate features two thick red stripes, one along the top and one along the bottom. It is the newest Baja California design, introduced in 2022, and is predominantly found in generation 4 coverage. If you're exploring recent Street View imagery of Baja California, this is the plate you'll most commonly encounter.

lm.name: Baja California Sur Orange - Baja California Sur Orange
lm.note: This plate is easily recognizable by its very thick orange stripe running along the top, making it one of the more straightforward plates to identify among Mexican states.

lm.name: Baja California Sur Purple - Baja California Sur Purple
lm.note: This plate is easily recognizable by its very thick purple stripe running along the top, making it one of the more straightforward plates to identify among Mexican states.

lm.name: Campeche - Campeche
lm.note: This plate features a multicolored stripe along the bottom, displaying a alternating array of colors. When the plate is unblurred, the stripe reveals a distinctive cityscape motif made up of small houses in various colors. It can be tricky to identify at a glance, but a good rule of thumb is: if you spot a white plate with a heavily multicolored bottom stripe, it is very likely from Campeche.

lm.name: Chiapas - Chiapas
lm.note: This plate is white with a distinctive colored corner on each of its four corners: yellow or orange on the upper left, green on the upper right, red on the lower left, and blue on the lower right. This four-color corner pattern makes it one of the most unique and easily recognizable plates among all Mexican states.

lm.name: Chihuaha blue - Chihuaha blue
lm.note: This plate is predominantly white, with a thick blue stripe running along the bottom. The blue band is centered at the lower portion of the plate and is quite clearly visible even from a distance. The rest of the plate is plain white with no other notable color elements.

lm.name: Chihuaha red - Chihuaha red
lm.note: This plate features a thick red stripe along the top, paired with a much thinner red line along the bottom. The contrast between the bold upper stripe and the subtle lower line is a useful detail to keep in mind when identifying this plate.

lm.name: Coahuila black line - Coahuila black line
lm.note: This is a relatively recent plate design, introduced in 2022, and is characterized by a thick black stripe along the bottom. It is commonly encountered in the newer Street View coverage of Coahuila.

lm.name: Colima brown - Colima brown green
lm.note: This is an older Colima plate design, but it appears frequently in the older Street View coverage of the state. The plate features a brown stripe on the bottom left and a green stripe on the bottom right. When the plate is blurred, these two stripes appear as a brown triangle and a green triangle, which can still serve as a useful identifying clue even at low resolution.

lm.name: Colima mexican flag - Colima mexican flag
lm.note: This is arguably one of the most recognizable Mexican state plates. It features a stripe along the bottom divided into the three colors of the Mexican flag: green on the left, white in the middle, and red on the right. Even when the plate is blurred, this tricolor band remains clearly visible, making it exceptionally easy to identify at a glance.

lm.name: Durango 23 - Durango new
lm.note: This is the newest Durango plate design, introduced in 2023, and is frequently found unblurred in Street View. Its most useful identifying feature is visible even when blurred: two orange dots, one on the bottom left and one on the bottom right of the plate. This plate is very common in the latest Street View coverage of Durango.

lm.name: Durango green line - Durango Red and Green
lm.note: This is an older Durango plate design, most commonly encountered in older Street View coverage, though it occasionally appears unblurred in more recent imagery as well. When blurred, the key identifying features are a red background in the center and a green stripe along the bottom.

lm.name: Durango yellow blue purple line - Durango yellow, blue and purple
lm.note: This white plate features a distinctive thin striped line along the bottom, made up of three colors in the following order: yellow, blue, and purple. Once you memorize this specific color sequence, the plate becomes very easy to identify. The combination is quite unique among Mexican state plates, making it one of the more memorable designs.

lm.name: Guanajuato - Guanajuato old
lm.note: This plate has a light-blue background with a thin red stripe. It is an older design, so it is predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of Guanajuato.

lm.name: Guerrero new plate - Guerrero new plate
lm.note: Introduced in 2022, this plate is straightforward to spot in the newer Street View coverage of Guerrero. When blurred, its most recognizable feature is a red dot on the bottom left and another on the bottom right, making it relatively easy to identify even at low resolution.

lm.name: guerrero old plate - Guerrero old plate
lm.note: This older Guerrero plate features yellow borders and a thick orange stripe along the bottom. It is predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of Guerrero.

lm.name: Hidalgo red line - Hidalgo new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Hidalgo plate design, introduced in 2023. When blurred, its key identifying feature is a thick dark red stripe along the bottom, which can sometimes appear purple depending on the image quality. This plate is widespread throughout the newer Street View coverage of Hidalgo.

lm.name: jalisco new plate - Jalisco new plate
lm.note: Jalisco has two recent plate designs one from 2019 and one from 2023 which are very similar to each other. Both share the same key identifying feature: a small thick stripe along the top of an otherwise white plate. When blurred, this stripe can appear either dark blue or dark green depending on the image. If you spot a white plate with a narrow but prominent top stripe in one of these dark tones, Jalisco is a strong guess.

lm.name: Jalisco old plate  - Jalisco old plate
lm.note: This is the older Jalisco plate design, predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of the state. It is one of the easier plates to recognize and remember, as it has a distinctly yellow top half and a blue bottom half, making it stand out clearly even in lower quality imagery.

lm.name: mexico state  - Estado de México
lm.note: This plate is predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of Estado de México but also can be seen in the new coverage. It has a bluish background with two red stripes: a thicker one along the top and a thinner one along the bottom. The combination of the blue background and dual red stripes makes it one of the easier plates to identify with confidence.

lm.name: Michoacan redline - Michoacán new
lm.note: This is the newest Michoacán plate design, introduced in 2022. Its most distinctive feature is a very thick stripe along the top, which can appear either dark red or purple depending on image quality. This plate is widely encountered throughout the newer Street View coverage of Michoacán.

lm.name: morelos - Morelos
lm.note: Morelos has two recent plate designs one from 2019 and one from 2022 which are very similar to each other. When blurred, both appear as a white plate with a large red dot on the bottom right. Once you know to look for that red dot on the right side, this plate becomes quite easy to identify.

lm.name: Nayarit 22 - Nayarit new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Nayarit plate design, introduced in 2022. It features a fairly thick multicolored stripe along the bottom, which can be tricky to identify when blurred. The key is to memorize the color order: light orange on the left, followed by blue and red in the middle, and green on the right. Remembering that the green is always on the right and the light orange always on the left is the most reliable way to distinguish this plate from others.

lm.name: New Nayarit purple line  - Nayarit Purple line
lm.note: Nayarit has two older plate designs, both featuring a thin purple stripe along the bottom. The earliest version, released in 2016, includes a mountain scene in the background, and when blurred its purple stripe takes on an unusual triangular shape. The second version, released in 2017, is simpler, displaying just a plain thin purple line at the bottom with no background imagery. Both designs are predominantly found in Street View coverage from 2016 to 2020.

lm.name: Nuevo Leon  - Nuevo Leon
lm.note: This plate is entirely white with no notable color elements, making it one of the plainest Mexican state plates. Even when blurred, faint black text remains visible in the center. Its stark, minimalist appearance makes it relatively straightforward to recognize once you are familiar with it.

lm.name: Old Nayarit - Nayarit old plate
lm.note: This is the oldest Nayarit plate design and quite distinctive. When blurred, it displays a prominent red triangle on the right side, making it relatively easy to identify at a glance. This plate is found exclusively in the older Street View coverage of Nayarit.

lm.name: old quintana roo  - Quintana Roo old plate
lm.note: This older Quintana Roo plate was introduced in 2011 and used until 2013. When blurred, it shows an orange stripe along with a black dot in the center. As expected given its age, it is found exclusively in the older Street View coverage of Quintana Roo.

lm.name: old veracruz - Veracruz old plate
lm.note: This is an older Veracruz plate, used approximately from 2015 to 2017, and commonly found throughout the older Street View coverage of the state. When blurred, it displays a multicolored stripe along the bottom in the following order: green and yellow on the left, a visible orange dot in the middle, and a yellowish or green tone on the right. This plate is frequently seen unblurred in Street View, making it one of the easier ones to identify with confidence.

lm.name: private truck veracruz - Veracruz private truck old plate
lm.note: This is a very old Veracruz plate design, used from 2011 to 2017, and commonly found throughout the older Street View coverage of the state. It was specifically issued for private trucks. When blurred, the most distinctive feature is a green stripe along the bottom with rounded shapes resembling hills. As with the other old Veracruz design, this plate is frequently seen unblurred in Street View, making it straightforward to identify.

lm.name: Puebla - Puebla new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Puebla plate design, introduced in 2020, and is widely found throughout the recent Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with a thick purple or dark red stripe that begins roughly in the middle of the plate and extends to the right. This distinctive half-stripe design makes it quite easy to recognize once you know what to look for.

lm.name: Queretaro - Querétaro new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Querétaro plate design, introduced in 2022, and is widely found throughout the recent Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with blue accents. When blurred, its most recognizable feature is a dark blue dot on the top left and another on the bottom right, creating a diagonal pattern that makes it quite easy to identify.

lm.name: San Luis Potosi - San Luis Potosi
lm.note: San Luis Potosí has two plate versions one from 2016 and one from 2019 which are very similar and appear identical when blurred. Both designs are found across old and new Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with a thick green stripe along the top, though notably the green does not extend all the way to the left edge, leaving a small white gap on the left side. This partial top stripe is the key detail to remember when identifying this plate.

lm.name: Sinaloa old plate - Sinaloa old plate
lm.note: In contrast to the newer design, this older Sinaloa plate is very easy to recognize. When blurred, a large red dot appears prominently in the center of the plate, giving it a striking resemblance to the Japanese flag. This design dates back to 2006 and was used until 2011, so it is only found in the oldest Street View coverage of Sinaloa.

lm.name: Sinaloa white - Sinaloa
lm.note: This is arguably the hardest Mexican state plate to identify. The plate is entirely white with only a very thin red stripe along the bottom. When blurred, it appears as an almost completely white plate with just a faint hint of red at the bottom edge. Even if the red is barely visible, that subtle touch of color at the bottom is enough to confidently identify it as a Sinaloa plate.

lm.name: Sonora old plate  - Sonora old plate
lm.note: This is an older Sonora plate design, used approximately from 2014 to 2017, and commonly found in the older Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with a very thin purple stripe along the bottom and a large orange dot on the right side. The combination of purple at the bottom and a prominent orange dot is the key detail to remember if you spot both of these features together, it is definitively a Sonora plate.

lm.name: Tamaulipas 19 - Tamaulipas
lm.note: This plate was introduced in 2019 and is white with a multicolored stripe along the bottom. The bottom line can be ambiguous, but the key pattern to remember is blue on the left and green in the middle and on the right. Even when blurred, keeping that simple color order in mind blue left, green right is enough to identify this plate with confidence.

lm.name: Tamaulipas new plate blue - Tamaulipas new plate blue
lm.note: This is the newest Tamaulipas plate design, introduced in 2022, and is widely found throughout the current Street View coverage of the state. The plate is predominantly white and blue. When blurred, it displays a thick blue stripe along the bottom that appears to be split by a small white dot in the center. This uniquely shaped blue stripe makes the plate quite easy to identify once you know what to look for.

lm.name: Tamaulipas new plate red - Tamaulipas new plate red
lm.note: This is the most recent Tamaulipas plate design, introduced in 2023, and is widely found throughout the current Street View coverage of the state. The plate is predominantly white and red. When blurred, it displays a thick red stripe along the bottom with a small black dot on the left side. That combination a red bottom stripe with a black dot on the left is the key detail that distinguishes it from the other mexican plates designs.

lm.name: Tlaxcala  - Tlaxcala new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Tlaxcala plate design and is widely found throughout the current Street View coverage of the state. The plate is predominantly white and purple. When blurred, it displays a thick purple stripe along the bottom with a dark blue section within it. The key distinguishing detail is a dark blue dot in the middle of that stripe so the overall pattern to remember is a purple bottom stripe with a dark blue dot at its center.

lm.name: Yucatan  - Yucatan old plate
lm.note: This is an older Yucatán plate design, used approximately from 2016 to 2019, and commonly found in the older Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with a thick green stripe along the top and a thinner green stripe along the bottom. The contrast between the bold upper stripe and the subtle lower line makes it fairly straightforward to identify.

lm.name: Zacatecas new  - Zacatecas new plate
lm.note: This is the newest Zacatecas plate design, introduced in 2022, and is widely found throughout the current Street View coverage of the state. The plate is predominantly white and red. When blurred, it displays a thick red stripe along the bottom that features a distinctive mountain shape, which can sometimes resemble a triangle. This uniquely shaped stripe is the key detail to remember once you familiarize yourself with its silhouette, this plate becomes quite recognizable.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note: These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector is sometimes seen, as well as a flat version.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Kilometer marker
lm.note: Mexican kilometer markers are black-rimmed white signs mounted at hip height, featuring the 'km' text and the kilometer number, both in black, arranged vertically.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Octagonal pole
lm.note:
Most utility poles in Mexico are made of CONCRETE and have an octagonal shape. Sometimes you can find them in Colombia so use different clues to make your guess.

If you see METAL octagonal pole you most likely will be in Philiphines.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Thick Arrows
lm.note: In Mexico, arrows on signs are noticeably thick compared to other countries in the Americas.

lm.name: Jalisco Taiwan/Kansai pole paint
lm.note: In the state of Jalisco, it is common to see poles painted Taiwan style with a black and yellow barberpole pattern, or Kansai style with long vertical black and yellow stripes. Careful: these can very rarely appear in other states

lm.note:

lm.name: Roadlines

lm.name: asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked
lm.note: Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.

lm.name: mesh body
lm.note: Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.

lm.name: single support
lm.note: Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.

lm.name: suspended below
lm.note: These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.

lm.name: white insulator
lm.note: White insulators that are shaped like acorns can be found along the coastal states of Mexico, but are by far most common in Michoacan, Colima, and Veracruz.

lm.name: wooden lowered crossbar
lm.note: Wooden poles with a lowered crossbar are mostly found in Sinaloa and Sonora.

lm.name: wooden suspended below
lm.note: The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.

top.html:
Most utility poles in Mexico are made of concrete and have an octagonal shape. There will often be engravings on the side.

NOTE: Octagonal poles are also common in Colombia.
top.raw: Most utility poles in Mexico are made of concrete and have an **octagonal shape**. There will often be engravings on the side. NOTE: Octagonal poles are also common in Colombia.

top.html:
Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs. Front plates are required.

NOTE: For an overview of the most common regional designs, see step 2.
top.raw: Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs. Front plates are required. NOTE: For an overview of the most common regional designs, see step 2.

top.html:
The most typical Mexican road lines are white solid outer lines with a single unbroken yellow middle line.

NOTE: Single broken yellow middle lines and double yellow middle lines are also common.
top.raw: The most typical Mexican road lines are white solid outer lines with a **single unbroken yellow middle line**. NOTE: [Single](https://goo.gl/maps/Dbjb5sJ1xcrQBTof7) broken yellow middle lines and [double](https://goo.gl/maps/L9YSqFc6h79idwkm8) yellow middle lines are also common.

top.html: These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector can sometimes be seen, as well as a flat version.
top.raw: These small, **cylindrical** white bollards with a **black base** are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector can sometimes be seen, as well as a flat version.

top.html: Mexico has two general road shields; one for national highways with “MEXICO” written at the top and a slightly curvy design, and one for state roads which have straight borders, and typically has the state initials written at the top.
top.raw: Mexico has two general road shields; one for national highways with “MEXICO” written at the top and a slightly curvy design, and one for state roads which have straight borders, and typically has the state initials written at the top.

top.html: Mexican directional signs have a distinctly large, all-caps white font.
top.raw: Mexican directional signs have a distinctly large, **all-caps** white font.

top.html: Mexican kilometre markers are white, with black font and outline.
top.raw: Mexican **kilometre markers** are white, with black font and outline.

top.html: Cacti, of many different species, are extremely common in Mexico.
top.raw: **Cacti**, of many different species, are extremely common in Mexico.

top.html:
Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs.

NOTE: All of South America, as well as Puerto Rico, use the word “PARE”. Panama, Costa Rica, and Guatemala also use “ALTO”.
top.raw: Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs. NOTE: All of South America, as well as Puerto Rico, use the word “PARE”. Panama, Costa Rica, and Guatemala also use “ALTO”.
Arrows on signs are noticeably **very thick**.

top.html: Yellow accents on kerbs and bridge barriers are quite common.
top.raw: **Yellow **accents on kerbs and bridge barriers are quite common.

top.html: You will commonly see wide cylindrical, black or white water tanks on rooftops.
top.raw: You will commonly see wide cylindrical, **black or white water tanks** on rooftops.
